newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Peace song divisive as Israel marks Rabin death.
newsitem.headline: Peace song divisive as Israel marks Rabin death.

text.p: Israeli youngsters left and right squabbled on Thursday over a peace song's lyrics ahead of a memorial for Yitzhak Rabin, showing that cracks in the society exposed by his assassination remained a year later.
Israelis observed the one-year anniversary of the prime minister's murder on Thursday according to the Jewish calendar.
In the slain leader's breast pocket, a bloodstained songsheet was found with the lyrics to the Hebrew "Song of Peace" he sang at a peace rally moments before his murder.

The gunman, Yigal Amir, was a religious Jew opposed to the Labour party leader's willingness to trade land Israel captured in 1967 -- land Amir believed God promised the Jewish people -- in exchange for peace with the Palestinians.
The musical director of the Tel Aviv Scouts youth group said the Song of Peace belonged in any memorial service for Rabin.
"The Song of Peace is the song most identified with Yitzhak Rabin," Yair Klinger told Israel Radio. "To do an event in his memory without singing the Song of Peace...is impossible."
But the right-wing Betar youth group said the song was too closely identified with the political left Rabin represented.
"We aren't ready to accept the whole web of ideology of the left at face value because the prime minister, may he rest in peace, was murdered," said Betar leader Eldad Halahmi.
Betar said it would respect those who sang the Song for Peace but would not add its voice to the chorus at a memorial planned for Sunday.
The song was used by the left-wing Meretz party as a campaign anthem before the May elections in which right-wing Likud leader Benjamin Netanyahu defeated Rabin's successor Shimon Peres.

Betar objected to a phrase in the song -- "let go of the fallen" -- which it said degraded the honour of Israel's fallen soldiers. A spokeswoman for the religious Bnei Akiva youth group said the Song for Peace contained "anti-religious" lyrics.
Israeli schools were a battleground for coming to grips with Rabin's legacy. In Jerusalem's secular Luria primary school, children on Thursday honoured Rabin with a moment of silence.
Students recalled memories of the murder. "I went to Rabin's grave and I lit a candle and I cried and I cried," said one flushed girl, fighting back nervous tears.

"One year ago Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was killed by a fanatic, Yigal Amir, who wore a skullcap. In the Torah he read every day it was written: Thou shalt not kill," 12-year-old Ariel Kedem told the assembly.
Israeli Education Minister Zevulun Hammer of the National Religious Party bristled at the suggestion that religious Israelis were collectively responsible for the murder.
"You cannot implicate an entire segment of the population," Hammer, appointed in June by Netanyahu, told Israel Television.
Israeli state religious schools observed the anniversary of Rabin's murder with special prayers, classes or assemblies. But ultra-Orthodox schools held courses as usual.

Many secular and leftist Israelis blame religious Jews who broadly opposed Rabin's peace policies for failing to speak out against right-wing demonstrators who branded Rabin a traitor and burned him in effigy before the assassination.
At Luria school, rightist photos depicting Rabin as a Nazi officer were displayed as a threat to democracy and tolerance.
"Current events show that tolerance is still not a part of Israeli society," said Luria English teacher Ellen Yishai.
Hammer skirted the issue when pressed on national television to state his programme for preventing future right-wing political violence.
"Bullets don't only fly from right to left...they fly both ways," Hammer insisted.
